question: A fast-growing e-commerce startup runs its checkout API on Cloud Run behind a global external Application Load Balancer. The SRE lead wants to define a single service level indicator (SLI) for the checkout API that directly reflects what customers experience, so that the team can later attach a service level objective (SLO) to it. Which SLI should you recommend?
options: The average CPU utilization of the Cloud Run service, measured every minute
The number of Cloud Run container instances that are running during peak hours
The proportion of checkout requests that return a 2xx response within 300 ms, measured at the load balancer
The number of deployments of the checkout service that complete without errors each week
explanation: A good SLI is a ratio of good events to total events that captures user-facing behavior; the fraction of requests that succeed within a latency threshold, measured as close to the user as possible (the load balancer), combines availability and latency into one customer-centric indicator. CPU utilization (option A) is a saturation signal useful for capacity, but customers do not experience CPU directly. Instance count (option B) is a resource metric, not a measure of service quality. Deployment success (option D) is a delivery metric and says nothing about how the service behaves for users. Under the Well-Architected Framework operational excellence and reliability pillars, SLIs should be derived from user-experience goals.
hint: Core Rule (SLIs and SLOs): A good SLI is a ratio of good events to total events that captures user-facing behavior; the fraction of requests that succeed within a latency threshold, measured as close to the user as possible (the load balancer), combines availability and latency into one customer-centric indicator.

question: A B2B SaaS company has agreed on a 99.9% 30-day availability SLO for its core API and has a written error budget policy. Two weeks into the month, a series of buggy releases has consumed the entire error budget. The product manager insists on shipping three new features this week because a major customer demo is scheduled. You are asked to advise the engineering director. What should you recommend?
options: Pause feature releases and dedicate the team to reliability work until the error budget is back within policy, as agreed in the error budget policy, escalating any exception to the executive sponsor
Lower the SLO to 99.5% for the remainder of the month so that the releases can proceed without breaching the objective
Ship the features but disable alerting on the SLO until the next 30-day window starts to avoid distracting the team
Deploy the features only to the region where the demo customer is located so that the rest of the fleet stays within budget
explanation: The whole point of an error budget policy is to remove the negotiation from the moment of crisis: when the budget is exhausted, the agreed consequence (typically a feature freeze in favor of reliability work) applies, and any exception must go through the documented escalation path rather than an ad-hoc decision. Lowering the SLO mid-window (option B) defeats the purpose of the objective and erodes trust in the process. Disabling alerts (option C) hides risk instead of managing it. Deploying to a subset of regions (option D) still spends budget the service does not have and adds inconsistency across the fleet. This is a core SRE practice highlighted in the operational excellence pillar under managing change.
hint: Core Rule (Error budgets): The whole point of an error budget policy is to remove the negotiation from the moment of crisis: when the budget is exhausted, the agreed consequence (typically a feature freeze in favor of reliability work) applies, and any exception must go through the documented escalation path rather than an ad-hoc decision.

question: A media company has just deployed a new video-transcoding microservice on GKE Autopilot. The platform team wants an initial dashboard that covers the four golden signals of monitoring recommended by Google SRE. They already have panels for request latency and error rate. Which two additional metrics should they add to complete the golden signals? (Choose two.)
options: Number of Git commits merged to the main branch per day
Pod CPU and memory utilization relative to the configured requests and limits
Number of nodes in the cluster over time
Total number of container image pulls per hour
Requests per second received by the service
Number of open pull requests in the service repository
explanation: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. Requests per second is the traffic signal (how much demand the service is receiving), and CPU/memory utilization relative to limits is the saturation signal (how full the service is). Commit and pull-request counts (options A and F) are delivery metrics, not runtime health signals. Node count (option C) and image pulls (option D) are infrastructure details that do not directly express demand or fullness of the service. Building dashboards around the golden signals is a recommended practice of the operational excellence pillar for detecting problems before they affect users.
hint: Core Rule: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.

question: A regional bank experienced a four-hour outage of its mobile banking backend after an engineer applied a firewall change that blocked traffic to Cloud SQL. The VP of Engineering has asked you to run the incident review and wants the report to name the engineer so that 'accountability is clear'. You want to follow Google SRE practices. What should you do?
options: Write the report naming the engineer, and recommend additional training and a formal warning to prevent recurrence
Skip the written report and instead hold a private conversation with the engineer and the VP to agree on corrective measures
Restrict the report to the technical timeline only, omitting any root-cause analysis so that no individual can be implicated

Conduct a blameless postmortem that focuses on the systemic conditions that allowed a single change to cause the outage, and track concrete action items such as peer-reviewed infrastructure-as-code changes and staged rollout of firewall rules
explanation: Blameless postmortems are a foundational SRE practice: they assume people acted with the best intent given the information they had, and they focus on why the system allowed a single action to cause an outage (no peer review, no staged rollout, no automated validation). Action items must be concrete, owned, and tracked to completion. Naming and punishing the engineer (option A) discourages people from reporting problems and hides the real systemic weaknesses. Avoiding a written report (option B) means the organization does not learn, and omitting root-cause analysis (option C) removes the most valuable part of the review. The Well-Architected Framework reliability pillar explicitly recommends conducting thorough, blameless postmortems.
hint: Core Rule: Blameless postmortems are a foundational SRE practice: they assume people acted with the best intent given the information they had, and they focus on why the system allowed a single action to cause an outage (no peer review, no staged rollout, no automated validation).

question: The operations team of a logistics company spends roughly 60% of its time on repetitive manual tasks: resizing persistent disks when a disk-full alert fires, renewing TLS certificates on Compute Engine web servers, and restarting VMs whose application process hangs. Engineers are burnt out, and project work keeps slipping. As the architect, you want to apply Google SRE guidance on toil. What should you recommend first?
options: Hire two additional operations engineers so that each engineer's share of manual work drops below 50%

Measure and categorize the toil, then eliminate the largest sources by engineering them away: move certificates to Google-managed certificates on a load balancer, enable managed instance group autohealing with application health checks, and automate disk expansion with an alerting policy that triggers a Cloud Run function
Create a detailed runbook for each of the three tasks so that junior engineers can perform them, freeing senior engineers for project work
Move all workloads to GKE Autopilot so that the operations team no longer manages any virtual machines
explanation: SRE defines toil as manual, repetitive, automatable work that scales with the service and has no enduring value, and Google recommends capping it at 50% of an engineer's time by measuring it and then engineering it away. The correct approach quantifies the toil and removes the top sources with automation and managed services: Google-managed certificates remove renewal work, MIG autohealing replaces manual restarts, and an alert-triggered Cloud Run function automates disk growth. Hiring more people (option A) scales the toil linearly rather than removing it. Runbooks (option C) make toil more consistent but do not reduce it, and they are a stepping stone to automation rather than the end goal. Replatforming everything to GKE Autopilot (option D) is a large, risky migration that is not justified by these specific tasks and would introduce new operational work.
hint: Core Rule (Toil reduction): SRE defines toil as manual, repetitive, automatable work that scales with the service and has no enduring value, and Google recommends capping it at 50% of an engineer's time by measuring it and then engineering it away.

question: A healthcare analytics company recently expanded its on-call rotation to include developers with limited operations experience. When a Cloud Monitoring alert fires at night, the new on-call engineers often do not know where to start, and mean time to resolve has doubled. You want to improve this with the least amount of operational overhead. What should you do?
options: Configure every alerting policy to notify the entire engineering team so that an experienced engineer is always available
Reduce the number of alerting policies to the three most critical ones so that new engineers only face familiar alerts
Add a playbook link and troubleshooting steps to the documentation field of each alerting policy so that the notification itself tells the on-call engineer what to check and how to mitigate
Require every new on-call engineer to complete a six-month shadowing period before taking a shift
explanation: Cloud Monitoring alerting policies include a documentation field that is rendered in the notification; using it to link a playbook (runbook) and list first-response steps gives on-call engineers immediate, actionable guidance at the moment they need it, which is a Google-recommended practice for incident management. Notifying everyone (option A) creates alert fatigue and blurs ownership. Deleting alerting policies (option B) reduces coverage rather than improving response. A six-month shadowing period (option D) is costly and does not scale, and it still leaves engineers without documentation when they are finally on their own.
hint: Core Rule (Runbooks and playbooks): Cloud Monitoring alerting policies include a documentation field that is rendered in the notification; using it to link a playbook (runbook) and list first-response steps gives on-call engineers immediate, actionable guidance at the moment they need it, which is a Google-recommended practice for incident management.

question: A global payments company has engineering teams in Singapore, Dublin, and São Paulo, but a single on-call rotation staffed only from Dublin covers all production services 24/7. Engineers report chronic night-time paging, and attrition is rising. Several recent incidents were prolonged because the on-call engineer was exhausted. You want to redesign the on-call model in line with Google SRE practices. What should you recommend?
options: Establish a follow-the-sun rotation across the three sites so that each team is paged only during its local working hours, set a maximum number of pages per shift, and review every alert to ensure it is symptom-based and actionable
Keep the single Dublin rotation but double the on-call compensation so that engineers are willing to accept the night-time pages
Outsource overnight monitoring to a third-party network operations center that escalates every alert to the Dublin engineer on duty
Suppress all non-critical alerting policies between 22:00 and 06:00 Dublin time so that the on-call engineer is not disturbed at night
explanation: Google SRE recommends distributing on-call across time zones (follow-the-sun) so that no one is routinely paged at night, capping the paging load per shift so responders have time to fix root causes, and periodically pruning alerts so only actionable, user-impacting symptoms page a human. Higher pay (option B) does not address fatigue or the resulting slower incident response. A NOC that escalates every alert (option C) simply adds a hop before the same tired engineer is woken up. Blanket alert suppression at night (option D) leaves real user-impacting incidents undetected and is not a substitute for alert hygiene.
hint: Core Rule (On-call management): Google SRE recommends distributing on-call across time zones (follow-the-sun) so that no one is routinely paged at night, capping the paging load per shift so responders have time to fix root causes, and periodically pruning alerts so only actionable, user-impacting symptoms page a human.

question: A retail chain runs a nightly Dataflow pipeline that loads point-of-sale data into BigQuery. Store managers rely on a Looker dashboard that must show the previous day's sales by 06:00 local time. The data engineering team wants to define an SLO for this pipeline that reflects the business expectation. Which SLI should the SLO be based on?
options: The average number of Dataflow worker VMs used by the pipeline each night
The percentage of Dataflow job launches that complete without a worker error in Cloud Logging
The 95th percentile of the pipeline's wall-clock duration in minutes
The percentage of days on which the complete previous-day dataset is queryable in BigQuery by 06:00
explanation: For batch and data pipelines, freshness and correctness are the user-facing SLI types; here the business only cares whether complete data is available by the deadline, so a freshness SLI measured as the fraction of days the deadline is met directly encodes the expectation. Worker count (option A) is a cost or capacity metric. Job launch success (option B) misses cases where the job succeeds but late or with incomplete data. Pipeline duration (option C) is a useful internal signal but a job that runs quickly yet starts late still misses the 06:00 deadline, so duration alone does not equal the user experience.
hint: Core Rule (SLIs for data pipelines): For batch and data pipelines, freshness and correctness are the user-facing SLI types; here the business only cares whether complete data is available by the deadline, so a freshness SLI measured as the fraction of days the deadline is met directly encodes the expectation.

question: An online travel company analyzed a year of postmortems and found that 70% of user-facing incidents were triggered by a production change, most often a deployment that was rolled out to all users at once. Leadership is considering a weekly change advisory board (CAB) that must approve every deployment. The company deploys roughly 40 times per day across 30 services and wants to keep that velocity. Which recommendation best reduces change-related incidents while preserving deployment frequency?
options: Introduce the weekly CAB but allow emergency changes to bypass it when an incident is already in progress

Adopt progressive delivery with Cloud Deploy: roll out each release as a canary to a small percentage of traffic, gate promotion on automated verification of SLIs, and automatically roll back on regression, so each change is small, observable, and reversible
Batch all changes into a single release every two weeks so that there are fewer risky change events per year
Require every change to be deployed simultaneously to all regions so that inconsistencies between regions cannot cause incidents
explanation: Google SRE and DORA research consistently show that reliability improves with smaller, more frequent, automatically verified changes that are easy to roll back, not with heavyweight approval gates. Progressive delivery (canary rollout with automated SLI verification and automated rollback) shrinks the blast radius of each change and detects regressions before they reach all users, which addresses the actual failure mode found in the postmortems. A CAB (option A) adds latency and manual toil without improving the technical safety of each change, and research links external approval boards with worse stability. Batching changes (option C) makes each release larger and harder to debug and roll back, increasing risk per release. Simultaneous global rollout (option D) maximizes blast radius, which is the opposite of what is needed.
hint: Core Rule (Change management for reliability): Google SRE and DORA research consistently show that reliability improves with smaller, more frequent, automatically verified changes that are easy to roll back, not with heavyweight approval gates.

question: A fintech startup is about to launch a new loan-origination service on GKE and Spanner and has asked the platform team to take over operational ownership after launch. The platform team wants to run a production readiness review (PRR) modeled on Google SRE practice before accepting the pager. Which three items should be mandatory outcomes of the PRR? (Choose three.)
options: The service has been load-tested to at least the forecast peak traffic with documented headroom, and autoscaling and quotas have been validated for that load
The service has been rewritten in the same programming language as the platform team's other services
SLIs and SLOs are defined, measured in Cloud Monitoring, and burn-rate alerting is configured to page the on-call rotation
The service runs in a single zone to keep the initial launch cost low until adoption is proven
Runbooks exist for every paging alert, and an on-call rotation with escalation paths has been agreed
All Spanner tables have been denormalized into a single table to simplify troubleshooting
explanation: A PRR verifies that a service can be operated reliably: it must have measurable objectives (SLIs/SLOs with alerting tied to the error budget), demonstrated capacity for expected load with headroom, and operational documentation plus staffed on-call and escalation. These map directly to the operational excellence pillar's readiness recommendations. Rewriting in another language (option B) is not a readiness criterion and would delay launch for no reliability gain. A single-zone deployment (option D) introduces an avoidable single point of failure and would normally be a PRR blocker rather than an outcome. Denormalizing Spanner into one table (option F) is a schema anti-pattern that harms performance and has nothing to do with operational readiness.
hint: Core Rule (Production readiness review): A PRR verifies that a service can be operated reliably: it must have measurable objectives (SLIs/SLOs with alerting tied to the error budget), demonstrated capacity for expected load with headroom, and operational documentation plus staffed on-call and escalation.

question: An insurance company's quote API has a 99.95% availability SLO. Every quote request synchronously calls an internal pricing service owned by another team, which only commits to a 99.9% SLO and has historically met it exactly. The quote API team keeps missing its own SLO even though its own code has had no defects. As the architect reviewing the design, what should you recommend?
options: Ask the pricing team to raise its SLO to 99.99% so that the quote API can meet its 99.95% target without design changes
Configure the quote API to retry failed pricing calls up to ten times without delay so that transient failures are masked

Recognize that a service cannot be more available than a hard synchronous dependency, and either decouple the dependency (for example, cache recent prices or serve a degraded default quote when pricing is unavailable) or renegotiate the quote API SLO to a realistic value
Move the pricing service into the same GKE cluster as the quote API to remove network hops and improve availability
explanation: Availability composes multiplicatively: a service with a hard synchronous dependency at 99.9% cannot honestly promise 99.95%, so the design must either remove the hard dependency (caching, graceful degradation, asynchronous patterns) or the SLO must be set realistically. This is the reliability pillar's guidance to set realistic targets and design for graceful degradation. Demanding a higher dependency SLO (option A) is not a design solution and may be impossible or very expensive for the other team. Aggressive retries without backoff (option B) amplify load during a pricing outage and can turn a partial failure into a cascading one. Co-locating services (option D) does not change the dependency's own failure rate and may reduce fault isolation.
hint: Core Rule (SLOs and dependencies): Availability composes multiplicatively: a service with a hard synchronous dependency at 99.9% cannot honestly promise 99.95%, so the design must either remove the hard dependency (caching, graceful degradation, asynchronous patterns) or the SLO must be set realistically.

question: A sporting-goods retailer runs its storefront on regional managed instance groups behind a global external Application Load Balancer. Last Black Friday, the site became unavailable because the MIG could not scale beyond the project's regional vCPU quota, and the team only discovered this during the event. This year the retailer expects five times normal traffic. What should you do to prepare?
options: Forecast peak demand, run load tests that reach the forecast with headroom, request quota increases well ahead of the event, and configure autoscaling with predictive or scheduled scaling to pre-provision capacity
Set the MIG maximum size to an unlimited value so that the autoscaler can add as many instances as needed on the day
Switch the storefront to preemptible Spot VMs so that the same budget buys more capacity during the event
Change the load balancer to a regional external Application Load Balancer so that traffic stays within one region and consumes less quota
explanation: Capacity planning is a core operational excellence practice: forecast demand, validate it with load testing, secure quota in advance (quota increases can take time and are not guaranteed instantly), and use predictive or scheduled autoscaling so capacity is ready before the surge. Raising the MIG size limit (option B) does nothing if the underlying quota is the constraint. Spot VMs (option C) can be reclaimed at any time and are unsuitable as the sole capacity for a revenue-critical event. Changing the load balancer scope (option D) does not reduce compute demand and would remove global failover.
hint: Core Rule: Capacity planning is a core operational excellence practice: forecast demand, validate it with load testing, secure quota in advance (quota increases can take time and are not guaranteed instantly), and use predictive or scheduled autoscaling so capacity is ready before the surge.

question: The head of product at a telehealth company states that the video-visit scheduling service must have 100% availability because 'patients depend on it'. question: A mobile ride-hailing app reports 99.99% availability on its server-side dashboards, computed from application logs on GKE. question: A manufacturing company creates a new Google Cloud project for each application team by clicking through the console. question: The on-call engineer at an ad-tech company receives about 200 pages per week. question: A subscription meal-kit company is planning a national television campaign that marketing estimates will drive a 20x surge in sign-ups for one hour. question: A startup is about to move its first production workload, a customer-facing API on GKE, from a proof of concept to general availability. The team has no monitoring beyond the default GKE dashboards, no defined alerts, and no documentation. The CTO asks what must be in place before launch to satisfy the operational readiness recommendations of the Well-Architected Framework operational excellence pillar. What should you tell the team?
options: Define SLIs and SLOs for the API, enable Cloud Observability with dashboards on the golden signals, configure actionable alerting policies with notification channels and playbooks, and document runbooks and an on-call escalation path before launch
Enable Cloud Armor and VPC Service Controls before launch; observability can be added after the first customers report problems
Purchase an Enhanced Support plan so that Google engineers can monitor the workload on the team's behalf
Increase the GKE node pool size by 50% so that capacity issues are unlikely during the launch period
explanation: The operational excellence pillar's readiness principle requires that a service be observable and operable before it takes production traffic: measurable objectives, dashboards and alerts on meaningful signals, notification routing, and documented runbooks and escalation paths. Security controls (option B) are important but belong to the security pillar and do not replace observability; waiting for customers to report problems is the opposite of readiness. A support plan (option C) provides Google assistance for Google Cloud issues; it does not monitor or operate the customer's application. Over-provisioning nodes (option D) addresses only one possible failure mode and does nothing for detection or response.

question: A cloud-based HR software vendor is about to sign its first enterprise contract, which includes a service level agreement (SLA) of 99.9% monthly availability with financial penalties for breaches. The engineering team proposes setting the internal SLO to exactly 99.9% so that 'the target matches the contract'. What should you advise?
options: Agree with the team; the SLO and the SLA should always be identical so that engineering and legal share one number

Set the internal SLO tighter than the SLA, for example 99.95%, so that the error budget alerts fire and reliability work starts before the contractual threshold is at risk, keeping a buffer between the internal objective and the external commitment
Set the internal SLO looser than the SLA, for example 99.5%, so that the engineering team is not constantly in a feature freeze
Do not define an SLO at all, because the SLA already defines the reliability target and a second number would be confusing
explanation: An SLA is an external promise with consequences; the internal SLO should be stricter so that the organization detects and reacts to reliability erosion while there is still margin before penalties apply. This buffer is standard SRE practice. Making the SLO equal to the SLA (option A) means that by the time the SLO is breached, the contract is already breached. A looser SLO (option C) would let the service routinely drop below the contractual threshold without triggering any response. Having no SLO (option D) leaves the team without an error budget to drive day-to-day decisions and without early-warning alerts.
